buildUp: Start with a big OLED touchscreen under toughened glass; it is the phone's face, its biggest power draw and the first thing that breaks if dropped.
The battery needs most of the space, so the computer shrinks onto one small, densely layered board, with memory stacked directly on the system-on-chip to save area and power.
Without a fan, heat from that chip must spread out, so it's pressed against a metal mid-plate that also stiffens the phone and gives everything a place to be fixed.
A metal body would block radio waves, so the aluminium frame is cut into insulated segments that themselves become the antennas for cellular, Wi-Fi, GPS and more.

Good photos need big sensors and long lenses that won't fit, so several small cameras with different focal lengths sit in a bump, some telephotos fold their light sideways with a prism, and the chip merges their results.
Glass on the back, rather than metal, lets a copper coil underneath pick up energy from a wireless charger, and sealed buttons and ports keep water out.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Where you can't make something bigger, make it smarter. One system-on-chip with specialised engines does each job with far less energy than a general processor, so tiny cameras can merge many frames into one good picture and the phone can run for a day. Everything else is packed in thin layers so the battery can fill most of the inside.

hardParts.title: Antennas in a metal phone
hardParts.why: A modern phone must talk on dozens of frequency bands, some with waves over 30 cm long, using antennas built from slices of a 15 cm frame that your hand keeps covering. Engineers tune the gaps and switch antenna circuits on the fly so the signal holds up whichever way you grip it.

hardParts.title: A desktop-class chip with no fan
hardParts.why: The system-on-chip can draw several times more power than the phone can shed, so it has to manage itself every millisecond: waking cores, choosing the right engine for each task and throttling before the case gets uncomfortable. The heat has to be spread across the whole phone so no single spot gets too hot.

hardParts.title: Real cameras in an 8 mm body
hardParts.why: A lens needs a certain distance between glass and sensor, and that distance grows with the sensor size, so a bigger, better sensor needs a thicker phone. Designers fight for every tenth of a millimetre, use prisms to lay long lenses sideways, and add moving stabilisation to the main camera, and even then the lenses stick out of the back.

principles.explanation: Switching energy grows with the square of the voltage, so running the chip at 0.7 V instead of 1 V roughly halves the energy of every operation. The cost comes from charging a tiny capacitor every time a transistor switches. Shrinking transistors to a 3 to 4 nm-class process makes each capacitor smaller still. Dedicated engines for graphics, images and AI help too: a circuit built for one job wastes far less energy than a general-purpose core working it out step by step.
principles.title: Lower voltage, far less energy

principles.explanation: With no fan, a phone can shed only a few watts through its skin, so the chip runs flat out only in short bursts and slows down when it stays hot. A phone can only lose heat from its surfaces, by radiation and by warming the air and your hand, and it has to keep its skin below about 45 degrees C. That limits steady power to a few watts, even though the chip can briefly draw 5 to 10 W. Each burst spreads its heat into the metal mid-plate, and the chip slows itself down if a heavy game or long video keeps it hot.
principles.title: No fan, so heat sets the speed

principles.explanation: Averaging several frames lets the true picture add up while random noise partly cancels, so the phone merges a burst of shots to make its tiny camera work in dim light. A phone camera pixel is tiny, so in dim light it catches only a few photons, and random arrival makes each count uncertain by about its square root, which shows as grain. Combining 9 frames cuts the noise to about a third. The phone captures a burst every time you press the shutter, lines up the frames to undo hand shake, and merges them.
principles.title: Averaging beats noise

principles.explanation: Each OLED pixel is a sandwich of thin organic layers that glow when current flows through them, so there's no backlight to leak. A black pixel is simply switched off, using no power, which gives true black and lets dark screens save energy. Modern panels can also slow their refresh rate when the picture isn't changing, from 120 times a second while scrolling down to as low as once a second for an always-on display.
principles.title: OLED: pixels that make their own light

firstPrinciples.problem: A phone is now most people's main camera, computer, map, wallet and television, and it still has to be about 8 mm thick, survive a day on one charge and never burn your hand. Cameras want big sensors and long lenses, chips want power and cooling, radios want room and no metal around them, and the battery wants all the space the others leave behind.

questions.answer: It can only lose a few watts of heat without a fan. Once it's warm, it lowers the chip's speed and voltage to protect the battery and keep the case comfortable, so performance drops.
questions.question: Why does a phone sometimes get slower after a long gaming session?

questions.answer: Each OLED pixel makes its own light, so a black pixel uses almost no power. An LCD's backlight stays on behind the whole screen no matter what it shows.
questions.question: Why does dark mode save battery on this phone, when it barely would on an older LCD phone?

questions.answer: A lens has to sit a certain distance from its sensor to focus an image, and bigger sensors need more distance. With the body only about 8 mm thick, there isn't room, so the camera module sticks out a few millimetres.
questions.question: Why can't the cameras be flush with the back?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The tiny lenses and sensors are a physical limit, and the leap has been in using computation to work around it. A modern phone photo is rarely one exposure. Before you even press the button the phone is buffering frames, and afterwards it aligns and blends several of them, recognises faces and sky, and adjusts each region separately, all in a fraction of a second.

name: Smartphone
overview:
A smartphone is a pocket computer with a radio, a camera and a screen you touch. Inside a case about 8 mm thick sits a complete computer on a single small circuit board: a system-on-chip with the processor, graphics and AI engines, memory and storage stacked on top of it, and radios for cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS and NFC.

Most of the inside isn't electronics at all; it's battery. A flat lithium-ion pouch takes up well over half the space, because everything the phone does, from lighting millions of OLED pixels to running the radios, comes down to how long that battery lasts. Wireless charging works through a flat copper coil behind the back glass, which picks up energy from a matching coil in the charger.

The screen is a stack: a sheet of toughened glass on top, a touch layer that senses your finger's electric charge, and an OLED panel whose pixels each make their own light. The aluminium frame around the edge holds it all together and is cut into sections that act as the phone's antennas. On the back, several tiny cameras with different lenses work together, and the phone's chip merges their pictures into one.

parts.description: Chemically toughened glass, or glass-ceramic, that protects the screen and survives most drops and scratches.

details.didYouKnow: Chemically toughened glass was developed in the early 1960s, more than 40 years before it became the face of the smartphone. Ordinary sand contains quartz, which is about as hard as the glass, which is why grit in a pocket can still leave fine scratches.
details.howItWorks: The cover glass is bonded to the display beneath it with an optically clear adhesive, so light passes straight through with almost no reflections between layers. Its toughness comes from a squeezed outer skin: when a crack tries to start at the surface, it first has to overcome that built-in compression. Your finger never touches the touch sensor directly; its electric field reaches through the glass instead.
keyNumbers: Typically about 0.5 to 0.8 mm thick
Compressed skin roughly tens of micrometres deep
About 6 to 7 on the Mohs hardness scale
details.madeOf: Aluminosilicate glass strengthened by soaking it in a hot bath of molten potassium salt, where big potassium ions swap in for smaller sodium ions and pack the surface tight. Some phones use a glass-ceramic with tiny crystals grown inside for extra drop resistance.

parts.name: Cover glass

parts.description: Flexible OLED panel where every pixel makes its own light, with a touch layer that senses your finger's charge.

details.didYouKnow: Because black OLED pixels are switched off completely, dark mode can noticeably cut screen power use, something that makes no difference on a backlit LCD.
details.howItWorks: Each pixel is made of red, green and blue specks of organic material that glow when a current flows through them, switched by a grid of thin-film transistors. Because there is no backlight, a black pixel is simply off. A mesh of transparent electrodes on top measures tiny changes in capacitance when a finger comes near, and the display can lower its refresh rate when nothing is moving to save power.
keyNumbers: About 6.1 to 6.3 inches diagonally
Up to about 120 refreshes per second
Roughly 450 to 460 pixels per inch
Peak brightness up to about 2,000 nits outdoors
details.madeOf: Organic light-emitting layers only a fraction of a micrometre thick, built on a flexible polyimide plastic base and sealed by thin barrier films. The seal matters because moisture and oxygen quickly ruin the organic layers.

parts.name: OLED display & touch layer

parts.description: Small selfie camera that looks out through a hole punched in the display.

details.didYouKnow: The preview you see while taking a selfie is usually mirrored like a looking-glass, because that feels natural, but many phones flip the saved photo back so text reads the right way round.
details.howItWorks: Light passes through the cover glass and a small hole cut through the OLED layers, then through a stack of tiny lenses onto an image sensor. The display software draws around the hole so it blends into the status bar. The same camera handles video calls, selfies and, on some phones, recognising your face to unlock.
keyNumbers: Typically about 12 MP
Aperture roughly f/1.9 to f/2.4
Records video up to about 4K
Hole in the screen only a few millimetres across
details.madeOf: A stack of moulded plastic lenses in a metal or plastic barrel over a silicon image sensor. Moulded plastic lets makers produce the unusual curved lens shapes cheaply and very precisely.

parts.name: Front camera

parts.description: Tiny speaker behind a slot above the screen for calls; it also plays the top half of stereo sound.

details.didYouKnow: A proximity sensor near the earpiece notices when your cheek comes close during a call and switches the touchscreen off, so you do not hang up with your face.
details.howItWorks: A tiny voice coil sits in the field of a magnet and pushes a thin diaphragm back and forth as the audio signal changes. During calls it plays quietly right into your ear; for music and videos it works with the bottom loudspeaker as a stereo pair, with software balancing the two very different speakers. A fine mesh over the slot keeps out dust and water.
keyNumbers: Driver typically about 1 cm long
Wideband call audio covers roughly 50 Hz to 7 kHz
Grille mesh holes a fraction of a millimetre wide
details.madeOf: A thin polymer diaphragm, a copper voice coil and a small neodymium magnet in a plastic housing. Neodymium magnets give a strong field from a very small, light piece of metal.

parts.name: Earpiece speaker

parts.description: Machined aluminium band round the edge; plastic-filled gaps split it into sections that work as antennas.

details.didYouKnow: Anodising does not paint the metal; it grows a layer of aluminium oxide out of the surface itself, and that oxide is far harder than the aluminium underneath.
details.howItWorks: The frame is the phone's spine: the front and back glass are glued to it, and it takes most of the bending and twisting when the phone is dropped or sat on. Thin breaks filled with plastic split the metal into separate pieces, and each piece is connected to the radios as an antenna tuned to particular frequency bands. The modem picks whichever antenna works best depending on how your hand is covering the phone.
keyNumbers: About 147 x 72 x 8 mm overall
Aluminium is roughly a third as dense as steel
Typically several separate antenna segments
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy machined from a solid block by computer-controlled cutters, then anodised for colour and scratch resistance. Aluminium is light, stiff, easy to machine and conducts radio signals well, which suits a frame that doubles as antennas.

parts.name: Aluminium frame

parts.description: Thin metal plate inside the frame that everything is screwed or glued to, and that spreads the chip's heat.

details.didYouKnow: When the phone gets too warm, it deliberately slows its processor and dims the screen; heat, not raw chip speed, is often what limits performance in long games.
details.howItWorks: The mid-plate runs across the inside of the frame and gives the display, logic board, battery and cameras something rigid to mount to. It also acts as a heat spreader: the processor's warmth is passed into it, often through graphite sheets or a flat vapour chamber, and spread out over the whole phone so no single spot gets too hot. Because a phone has no fan, this passive spreading is the main way it keeps cool.
keyNumbers: Typically under 1 mm thick
Processor bursts can reach roughly 5 to 10 W of heat
Surface usually kept below about 45 degrees C
details.madeOf: Aluminium, usually machined as part of the frame or attached to it. Aluminium conducts heat well and is light, and thin graphite sheets are often added because they spread heat sideways even better.

parts.name: Internal mid-plate

parts.description: Button for turning the volume up; a tiny switch inside clicks against a flex cable.

details.didYouKnow: In the camera app, the volume up button usually works as a shutter button, which is handy for holding the phone like a real camera.
details.howItWorks: The metal button cap sits in a sealed hole in the frame and presses on a tiny dome switch mounted on a thin flex cable behind it. When the dome collapses it closes a circuit and gives that crisp click, and the flex cable carries the signal to the logic board. A rubber or silicone seal around the button keeps water out.
keyNumbers: Travel typically only a fraction of a millimetre
Typically rated for well over 100,000 presses
Volume usually set in about 15 to 30 steps
details.madeOf: A machined aluminium cap matching the frame, over a stainless steel dome switch on a polyimide flex cable. The steel dome springs back reliably for many thousands of presses.

parts.name: Volume up button

parts.description: Button for turning the volume down.

details.didYouKnow: On many phones, pressing volume down together with the side button takes a screenshot, a shortcut that works even when an app freezes the screen.
details.howItWorks: This button shares the same flex cable as volume up, with its own dome switch underneath, so the two are often replaced as one part. Pressing it lowers the volume of whatever is playing, or the ringer if nothing is. Combined with other buttons it also triggers system functions such as screenshots or forced restarts.
keyNumbers: Dome switch roughly 3 to 5 mm across
Typically rated for well over 100,000 presses
Sealed for water resistance down to about 6 m on many flagships
details.madeOf: Machined aluminium, anodised to match the frame, with a small seal to keep out water. The dome switch underneath is thin stainless steel.

parts.name: Volume down button

parts.description: Wakes and locks the phone; held down, it summons the assistant or powers off.

details.didYouKnow: On many phones, pressing the side button five times quickly starts an emergency SOS call, a feature designed for situations where you cannot unlock the screen.
details.howItWorks: A single short press sends a signal to the power management chip and processor to wake or lock the screen, which only takes a moment because the phone is never truly off while sleeping. A long press is timed by the system and passed to the voice assistant or the power-off menu. On some phones the button also hides a fingerprint sensor.
keyNumbers: Typically rated for well over 100,000 presses
Long press usually about 1 to 2 seconds
Fingerprint sensors in buttons often around 4 mm wide
details.madeOf: Aluminium or stainless steel, larger than the volume buttons, over a dome switch on a flex cable. Its seal is designed to keep water out while still allowing a firm click.

parts.name: Side (power) button

parts.description: Tray that pops out with a pin to hold a SIM card, though many phones now rely on a built-in eSIM.

details.didYouKnow: The first SIM cards in the early 1990s were the size of a credit card; the nano-SIM is a small fraction of that size and still uses the same basic contact layout.
details.howItWorks: Pushing a pin into the little hole releases a spring catch so the tray slides out. The SIM's gold contacts then press against spring contacts on a reader inside the phone, which talks to the modem to prove to the network who you are. An eSIM does the same job with a chip soldered to the board, onto which carrier profiles are downloaded.
keyNumbers: Nano-SIM about 12.3 x 8.8 mm
Nano-SIM about 0.67 mm thick
An eSIM can typically store several carrier profiles
details.madeOf: An aluminium or stainless steel tray with a rubber gasket round its outer face. The gasket keeps water out of the hole when the tray is closed.

parts.name: SIM tray

parts.description: Dense, double-stacked circuit board: the whole computer and every radio on a board smaller than a playing card.

details.didYouKnow: Stacking the board in two layers roughly halves its footprint, and almost all of the space saved goes to a bigger battery.
details.howItWorks: The logic board carries the processor, memory, radios and power chips and links them with wiring hidden in many thin layers. To save space it is often built as two boards stacked like a sandwich and joined round the edge by a frame of connections called an interposer. Flex cables plug into it from the display, battery, cameras and buttons.
keyNumbers: Typically about 10 or more copper layers
Often more than 1,000 components
Smallest parts about 0.4 x 0.2 mm
details.madeOf: Layers of glass-fibre-reinforced epoxy with fine copper wiring between them, joined by tiny laser-drilled holes. The parts are soldered on with lead-free solder, and metal shields cover the radio chips to stop interference.

parts.name: Logic board

parts.description: The processor, graphics, AI engine and image processor on a single chip, made with transistors only a few nanometres across.

details.didYouKnow: The 3 nm in a process name is a marketing label rather than a measurement; no feature on the chip is actually 3 nanometres wide, though the transistors really are astonishingly small.
details.howItWorks: The system-on-chip combines the main processor cores, the graphics processor, a neural engine for AI tasks and an image signal processor that turns raw camera data into photos. It mixes a few fast performance cores with several frugal efficiency cores and shifts work between them to save battery. The RAM is often stacked directly on top of it in the same package so data has the shortest possible path.
keyNumbers: Roughly 15 to 20 billion transistors
Built on a 3 to 4 nm-class process
Top cores run at about 3 to 4 GHz
Typically about 8 GB of RAM stacked alongside
details.madeOf: A silicon die patterned with billions of transistors and many layers of copper wiring, sealed in a package with the memory. Silicon is used because its electrical behaviour can be controlled precisely by adding tiny amounts of other elements.

parts.name: System-on-chip

parts.description: Flash memory that keeps your apps, photos and files when the power is off.

details.didYouKnow: Flash memory was invented in the early 1980s by engineer Fujio Masuoka, and it was supposedly named because erasing it in one go reminded a colleague of a camera flash.
details.howItWorks: Flash storage keeps data by trapping electric charge in billions of tiny cells, and the amount of charge in each cell stands for several bits. The cells are stacked in hundreds of layers like a skyscraper to fit more into the same area. A built-in controller spreads writes evenly across cells, because each one wears out slowly with use.
keyNumbers: Typically 128 GB to 1 TB
Reads at up to about 4 GB per second
Often more than 200 layers of cells
Usually 3 bits stored per cell
details.madeOf: Silicon chips of 3D NAND flash memory, several stacked in one package with a controller chip. Flash is used because it keeps data with no power and has no moving parts.

parts.name: Storage chip

parts.description: Chips that handle 5G, LTE, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS, switching between antennas as you hold the phone.

details.didYouKnow: GPS works only because engineers correct for Einstein's relativity: the satellites' clocks drift by about 38 microseconds a day compared with clocks on the ground, which would add kilometres of error.
details.howItWorks: The modem turns data into radio signals and back, following the rules of 5G and LTE networks. A transceiver shifts signals to the right frequency, power amplifiers boost them, and filters keep dozens of bands from interfering with each other. Separate chips handle Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS and NFC, all sharing the antennas built into the frame.
keyNumbers: Phone transmit power up to about 0.2 W
Supports typically dozens of frequency bands
5G peak speeds up to several gigabits per second
GPS satellites orbit about 20,200 km up
details.madeOf: Silicon chips plus special materials such as gallium arsenide in some power amplifiers and piezoelectric crystals in the filters. Each material is chosen for how well it handles high-frequency signals.

parts.name: Modem & radio chips

parts.description: Controls charging and supplies dozens of precisely regulated voltages to the other chips.

details.didYouKnow: Fast charging deliberately slows down as the battery nears full, and many phones pause near 80 percent overnight to reduce wear on the cell.
details.howItWorks: The power management chip takes energy from the battery or charger and converts it into many separate supply voltages using tiny, fast-switching converters. It can turn whole sections of the phone off in a fraction of a second when they are not needed. It also manages charging, pushing current in fast at first and then easing off as the battery fills.
keyNumbers: Processor cores often run below about 1 V
Battery charged to about 4.4 V when full
Wired charging typically about 20 to 45 W
Converters switch millions of times per second
details.madeOf: A silicon chip working with small inductors and capacitors on the logic board. Switching converters are used because they waste far less energy than simply burning off extra voltage as heat.

parts.name: Power management chip

parts.description: Linear vibration motor that makes the crisp clicks and buzzes you feel when you type or get a notification.

details.didYouKnow: Older phones vibrated using a tiny spinning motor with an off-centre weight, which took time to spin up and down and could only make a mushy buzz.
details.howItWorks: Inside is a small weight on springs with a magnet and coil, which shoves the weight back and forth in a straight line. Driving it at its natural bouncing frequency gives strong vibration from little power, and driving it in reverse stops it almost instantly. That quick start and stop is what lets the phone make short, precise taps instead of a long buzz.
keyNumbers: Natural frequency roughly 150 to 250 Hz
Weighs typically a few grams
Starts and stops in about tens of milliseconds
details.madeOf: A dense metal mass, often tungsten or steel, with neodymium magnets, a copper coil and steel springs in a metal case. A heavy mass in a small space gives a stronger kick.

parts.name: Haptic motor

parts.description: Main speaker at the bottom, in a sealed box that acts like a tiny hi-fi enclosure.

details.didYouKnow: Some phones can play a special low tone that shakes water droplets out of the speaker grille after the phone gets wet.
details.howItWorks: A small driver pushes air out of the grille at the bottom of the phone, while a sealed space behind it acts as a box that stops the back wave cancelling the front. A smart amplifier watches the speaker's movement and temperature as it plays, letting it run louder without damage. Software boosts the bass as far as a speaker this small can manage.
keyNumbers: Driver about 1 to 2 cm long
Back volume roughly 1 cubic centimetre
Bass fades below roughly 300 to 500 Hz
details.madeOf: A polymer diaphragm, copper coil and neodymium magnet in a plastic enclosure, with a water-resistant mesh over the opening. Plastic lets the enclosure be moulded into whatever space is left beside the battery.

parts.name: Loudspeaker

parts.description: Reversible connector for charging and data, sealed against water.

details.didYouKnow: European Union rules made USB-C the required charging port for new phones sold there from the end of 2024, to cut down on drawers full of different chargers.
details.howItWorks: The port has a central tongue with contacts on both sides, so a plug works either way up. When a charger is plugged in, the phone and charger talk to each other over dedicated pins to agree how much voltage and current is safe. The same port carries data, audio and sometimes video out.
keyNumbers: 24 contact positions
Opening about 8.3 x 2.5 mm
Rated for about 10,000 insertions
Spec allows up to 240 W, phones use far less
details.madeOf: A stainless steel shell around a plastic tongue with gold-plated contacts, sealed with a gasket where it meets the frame. Steel survives repeated plugging, and gold resists corrosion.

parts.name: USB-C port

parts.description: Several tiny MEMS microphones whose signals are combined to cancel background noise on calls.

details.didYouKnow: MEMS microphones are etched on silicon wafers by the thousand, which is why a phone can afford several of them for the price of one old-style microphone.
details.howItWorks: Each microphone has a tiny silicon diaphragm next to a fixed plate; sound waves move the diaphragm and change the electrical capacitance between them. The phone compares what the different microphones hear and uses the tiny time differences to focus on your voice and subtract background noise. Rear and top microphones also record stereo sound for video.
keyNumbers: Typically 3 or 4 microphones
Each package roughly 3 x 2 x 1 mm
Diaphragm typically under 1 mm across
details.madeOf: Silicon MEMS chips, made with the same techniques as processors, in small metal-lidded packages with a matching amplifier chip. Water-resistant membranes cover the sound holes.

parts.name: Microphones

parts.description: Flat lithium-ion pouch cell that fills most of the phone; it's held in with pull-tab adhesive strips for repairs.

details.didYouKnow: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino for developing the lithium-ion battery, which first went on sale in 1991.
details.howItWorks: When charging, lithium ions are pushed out of the cathode and tucked between layers of graphite in the anode; when you use the phone they flow back, and the electrons go the long way round through your phone's circuits. A thin porous separator keeps the two electrodes from touching. A small protection circuit on the cell cuts it off if it is overcharged, overheated or shorted.
keyNumbers: About 3,500 to 4,500 mAh
Roughly 3.85 V nominal
About 13 to 17 Wh of energy
Keeps roughly 80 percent after 500 to 1,000 cycles
details.madeOf: Graphite on copper foil for the anode, lithium cobalt oxide on aluminium foil for the cathode, a plastic separator and liquid electrolyte, all sealed in an aluminium laminate pouch. A pouch wastes less space than a hard can.

parts.name: Battery

parts.description: Flat spiral of copper behind the back glass that picks up energy from a charging pad, with a ring of magnets to align it.

details.didYouKnow: The common wireless charging standard is called Qi, from the Chinese word for the flow of energy, and is pronounced 'chee'.
details.howItWorks: A coil in the charging pad makes a rapidly changing magnetic field, and this flat coil picks it up and turns it back into electricity, like the two halves of a transformer. The phone and pad talk to each other through the same field to agree how much power to send. A ring of magnets snaps the phone into the best spot, and a ferrite sheet stops the field heating the battery behind it.
keyNumbers: Up to about 15 W
Field alternates roughly 100,000 to 200,000 times a second
Coil roughly 40 to 50 mm across
details.madeOf: Fine copper wire wound into a flat spiral on a magnetic ferrite sheet, with small neodymium magnets around it. Copper conducts well, and ferrite guides the magnetic field where it is wanted.

parts.name: Wireless charging coil

parts.description: Wide camera with the biggest sensor and optical stabilisation; it takes most of your photos.

details.didYouKnow: Many phones begin capturing frames before you tap the shutter, so the final photo can include detail from a moment that had already happened.
details.howItWorks: This camera's large sensor gathers the most light, and usually combines groups of four neighbouring pixels into one for cleaner photos in dim light. Optical stabilisation shifts the lens or the sensor itself to cancel out hand shake. For each photo the image processor often merges several frames taken in quick succession to stretch the brightness range and cut noise.
keyNumbers: About 48 to 50 MP
Aperture roughly f/1.6 to f/1.9
About 24 mm equivalent focal length
Usually saves 12 MP photos by default
details.madeOf: A stack of about six or seven moulded plastic lens elements, sometimes with a glass element, over a silicon image sensor. Small motors and magnets move the parts for focus and stabilisation.

parts.name: Main camera

parts.description: Camera with a very wide-angle lens for landscapes, rooms and close-up macro shots.

details.didYouKnow: A raw ultra-wide image bulges like a fisheye; the straight lines you see are the result of software reshaping every pixel after the shot.
details.howItWorks: A short focal length lens squeezes a very wide view onto a smaller sensor, so you can fit in a whole room or landscape from where you stand. The edges come out curved, so software stretches them straight again. With autofocus it can also focus very close, which is why many phones switch to it for macro shots.
keyNumbers: About 13 mm equivalent focal length
Field of view roughly 120 degrees
Typically 12 to 48 MP
Macro focus down to about 2 cm
details.madeOf: A compact stack of moulded plastic lenses with strongly curved shapes over a silicon sensor. Plastic aspheric lenses are what make such a wide view possible in so little depth.

parts.name: Ultra-wide camera

parts.description: Zoom camera, often using a prism to fold a longer lens sideways inside the thin body.

details.didYouKnow: Zooming in on a phone is mostly switching between separate cameras; only the in-between steps and the highest zoom levels are digital crops.
details.howItWorks: A long lens is needed to magnify distant subjects, so many phones use a prism to bend the light sideways and lay the lens along the body, like a periscope. It usually has its own stabilisation because small hand shakes are magnified too. When you choose a zoom level between the cameras' fixed steps, the phone crops and blends images from the nearest one.
keyNumbers: About 3x to 5x optical zoom
Roughly 77 to 120 mm equivalent focal length
Typically about 12 MP
Aperture around f/2.8
details.madeOf: Moulded lenses, a glass prism or mirror and a silicon sensor in a long metal-and-plastic module. Glass is used for the prism because it bends light precisely and stays stable.

parts.name: Telephoto camera

parts.description: LED flash, plus a small sensor that measures distance with infrared light to help focus and portrait shots.

details.didYouKnow: To measure distance by timing light, the sensor must measure gaps of well under a billionth of a second, since light covers a metre there and back in about 7 nanoseconds.
details.howItWorks: The flash is a bright white LED that fires in sync with the camera and doubles as the torch. The depth sensor sends out invisible infrared light and times how long it takes to bounce back, building a rough map of how far away things are. That map helps the cameras focus fast in the dark and separate a person from the background in portrait shots.
keyNumbers: Depth range up to about 5 m
Light travels about 30 cm per nanosecond
Flash useful to roughly 2 to 3 m
details.madeOf: LED chips coated in phosphor that turns blue light into white, under a plastic or glass lens. The depth sensor pairs an infrared laser emitter with a special light-timing sensor.

parts.name: Flash & depth sensor

parts.description: Glass back that lets wireless charging work through it, with a frosted finish.

details.didYouKnow: The frosted finish is made by etching the glass with acid, which also helps hide fingerprints compared with shiny glass.
details.howItWorks: The back glass closes the phone and lets the magnetic field from a wireless charger pass straight through to the coil inside, which a solid metal back would block. It is glued to the frame with adhesive that also helps seal out water. Repair shops often loosen it with heat or lasers because the adhesive is so strong.
keyNumbers: Typically about 0.5 to 0.8 mm thick
Lets through wireless charging up to about 15 W
Phone weighs about 170 to 200 g in total
details.madeOf: Chemically toughened glass, like the front, with colour layers on the inside. The matte look comes from etching the surface.

parts.name: Back glass

parts.description: Raised glass-and-metal plateau that protects the lenses, which are too long to fit inside the thin body.

details.didYouKnow: Sapphire is one of the hardest natural materials, far harder than glass, but the sapphire on phones is grown in factories, not mined.
details.howItWorks: Big sensors need lenses set further from the sensor, and that distance is longer than the phone is thick, so the camera modules poke out the back. The bump gives them a strong metal surround and protective windows over each lens. Its raised edge also keeps the lens covers off the table when the phone lies flat.
keyNumbers: Sticks out roughly 2 to 4 mm
Body only about 8 mm thick
Sapphire scores 9 on the Mohs scale
details.madeOf: An aluminium surround with lens windows of sapphire crystal or toughened glass. Sapphire is chosen for its exceptional scratch resistance.

parts.name: Camera bump

summary: A modern smartphone: an OLED touchscreen under toughened glass, an aluminium frame that doubles as antennas, a logic board packed with a powerful chip, and a battery that fills most of the space inside.
